episode_title: The Business of Trucking: Lessons from 22 Years in the Industry

real_qa.q: Why did Tristan Bordello close I Am Freight after seven years of operation?
real_qa.r: Tristan closed I Am Freight in May 2026 due to sustained market pressures and thin margins in the asset-based trucking sector. He emphasized that hope only lasts so long before reality hits, and despite attempting to outrun the downturn, he realized the cards were not going to play in the right direction. His primary concern throughout the process was protecting his personal guarantee and avoiding bankruptcy, which took a full year of conversations before the actual shutdown.
real_qa.requete: Why did Tristan Bordello close I Am Freight

real_qa.q: What are the main cash flow challenges for asset-based trucking carriers in 2024-2026?
real_qa.r: Trucking carriers face severe cash flow problems driven by thin margins, rising operational costs, and customer concentration risk. Tristan explained that one major customer delayed a large payable for months while fuel prices spiked, and carriers must maintain cash reserves to cover operations before insurance claims are paid out. Additionally, fuel, insurance premiums, and vehicle registration all increase annually and hit simultaneously, devastating cash reserves—even profitable companies can fail if they lack sufficient cash to bridge these periods.

real_qa.q: What is the difference between knowing trucking operating costs and actual market profitability?
real_qa.r: Knowing your costs as an owner and having the market pay for those costs with profitability are two different things. The market determines what customers will pay, and if there is oversupply of carriers willing to operate below cost, individual carriers cannot force higher rates. Tristan illustrated this by noting that brokers paying five dollars per mile outbound from California often only pay seventy cents to one dollar per mile on the return, making it impossible to be profitable despite knowing the true cost to operate.
real_qa.requete: Trucking operating costs versus market rates

real_qa.q: How should trucking company owners approach equipment valuations when considering a sale?
real_qa.r: When Tristan attempted to sell I Am Freight, he discovered that equipment valuations often exceed what a buyer will offer for the entire business. Buyers underwrite businesses based on cash flow and future earning potential, not asset replacement value. After reaching out to his network and evaluating the company with legal counsel, he realized his equipment was worth more than the sale offer, which led him to decide closing was preferable to selling at a loss.

real_qa.q: What clarity do founders gain after making the difficult decision to close a business?
real_qa.r: After closing I Am Freight, Tristan experienced unexpected mental and physical relief—he slept significantly more, was able to work out regularly, and felt mentally clearer. He realized that when you are deep in the constant chaos of running an asset-based business, that chaos feels normal, but once everything stops, the quiet reveals how much strain the daily problems created. This calm after the storm enabled him to reflect on decisions more decisively and to rethink his exit strategy for his remaining brokerage business.
real_qa.requete: Closing a business mental clarity relief

real_qa.q: How should founders design their brokerage business models with an exit strategy in mind?
real_qa.r: Tristan learned that designing a company to be sellable is very different from running a lifestyle business. He is now rethinking Freightopia with exit strategy in mind—asking how to structure it so it is not just a vehicle dependent on his personal effort. This requires understanding what creates value in a business and making decisions that build enterprise value, not just personal income. As he noted, whether you exit soon or much later, every decision should be made with the eventual sale or transition in mind.

guest.bio_context: Tristan Bordello built Freightopia, a freight brokerage, over many years and also founded I Am Freight, an asset-based trucking company with a mission focused on drivers. In May 2026, he closed the trucking company after seven years of operation while continuing to operate his brokerage. He previously appeared on the Driving Forward Podcast in August 2024, approximately two years before this episode.
